newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical employers object to 1997 pay claim.
newsitem.headline: German chemical employers object to 1997 pay claim.

text.p: German wage talks in the chemical sector made little early progress on Tuesday as employers disputed the basis for the 1997 wage claim made by union negotiators.

The IG Chemie trade union had earlier said it would be going into the talks seeking a 4.2 percent overall rise in wages, reflecting productivity growth of 2.7 percent in the industry and an estimated 1.5 percent rate of inflation.

But leaders of the BAVC chemical employers federation told journalists during a break in talks they did not accept the level of the productivity rise because it had only been obtained as a result of job cuts.
"(That factor) cannot therefore be used for wage increases," BAVC chief negotiator Hans Paul Frey said.
Both sides said however that talks, which broke up for lunch, had not yet reached the stage of concrete negotiations.
Negotiations started earlier in a bid to solve a dispute on possible sick pay cuts, which threatens to disrupt the normally good relations in the industry.

Both IG Chemie and DAG, the white-collar workers union, stressed that they would be seeking to retain full sick pay entitlements, which under a new law would be cut to 80 percent of salary from 100 percent.
IG Chemie chief negotiator Hans Terbrack said in a reference to possible protest action that if no agreement was reached on that issue "there was enough pressure in the factories to cause a fuss".

Wage contracts for the some 590,000 west German chemcials workers in the west German do not specifically protect sick pay at 100 percent of salary in the same way that metal and engineering unions argue that contracts in their sectors do.

Nonetheless, a recent attempt by BASF AG to implement the cuts led to mass protests from its workers in an industry that normally prides itself on being able swiftly to come to agreements between employers and workers.
IG Chemie said it was willing to consider reductions in holiday bonuses in an overall agreement as long as full sick pay entitlements were secured.
The BAVC said last month that companies would have to decide for themselves whether they would implement the sick pay cuts until a sector-wide agreement could be found.
IG Chemie said late last month that it knew of no large company that had so far sought to put the new law into effect.
The talks are due to continue on Tuesday.
